title: Orchard and Typewriter
premise: In 1917, in a river town turned garrison, battlefield nurse Ines Eriksen secretly records the names of soldiers the officers' official reports omit — the deserters shot, the dead listed as missing, the men erased for convenience. When the army requisitions the town's print workshop to destroy its archives and produce sanitized casualty lists, Ines discovers her ledger has been seized along with everything else. Racing against the spring thaw that will let the army ship the evidence downriver and burn the rest, she allies with the printer's orphaned apprentice, a disgraced clerk, and an aging officer who once signed the omissions himself. The book ends with Ines printing the true names on the workshop's last usable press the night before demolition, distributing them through the town before the ice breaks; the workshop falls, but the ledger survives in a thousand hands, and Ines finally writes her own name at the end of it.
about_author: Juniper Halloran is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing wartime correspondence in municipal basements across northern Europe. Orchard and Typewriter is her second novel, written in a converted cider house where she keeps a 1912 typewriter that jams on the letter Q.

chapters.title: The Ledger Under the Floorboards
chapters.summary: Ines Eriksen's POV. Returning from the front hospital to the river town, Ines hides her private ledger of omitted names beneath the orchard house floorboards and resumes quiet work mending bandages. She observes how the town has learned not to ask questions. Emotional beat: weary vigilance, the comfort of small routines concealing dangerous knowledge.

chapters.title: Requisition Papers
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Army officers arrive and post requisition orders: the print workshop, the granary, and all private papers are claimed for the war effort. Ines watches soldiers carry crates out of the workshop while the printer, old Marek, protests and is struck down. Emotional beat: dread hardening into resolve as she realizes what 'all papers' might include.

chapters.title: What the Officers Omit
chapters.summary: Ines's POV, with a flashback to the field hospital where she began recording names. She recalls Corporal Voss, listed as missing though she held his hand as he died, and explains why she started the ledger. Emotional beat: grief transmuted into purpose; memory as an act of defiance.

chapters.title: The Apprentice
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Sixteen-year-old Tomas, Marek's apprentice, tends the presses under military supervision and notices a nurse asking careful questions about which crates go where. He says nothing, but begins his own silent count of what is being destroyed. Emotional beat: cautious curiosity, two watchers recognizing each other without speaking.

chapters.title: The Clerk Who Signed
chapters.summary: Aldous Brandt's POV. A disgraced army clerk, Brandt arrives to inventory the seized documents and recognizes the ledger's format — he once processed the very omission reports it contradicts. Haunted by a name he falsified years ago, he hesitates over Ines's entry. Emotional beat: guilt surfacing after long suppression.

chapters.title: Ice on the River
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Ines learns the ice will break within weeks, and with it the barges will come to haul the archive away for burning downstream. She visits the workshop openly, volunteering as a medic for the garrison, and sees her ledger locked in the records room. Emotional beat: the clock starts ticking; fear sharpened into planning.

chapters.title: An Alliance of Small Treasons
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converging. Ines, Tomas, and Brandt meet awkwardly in the workshop's back room; each reveals a piece of what they know. None fully trusts the others, but they agree the ledger must not leave on the barges. Emotional beat: fragile found family forming out of mutual need.

chapters.title: The Orchard House
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Ines brings Tomas and Brandt home to the orchard house for a supper of preserved apples, and shows them the hiding place under the floorboards — empty now, but proof of what she risked. They map the workshop together. Emotional beat: warmth and domesticity briefly outweighing danger; the found family takes root.

chapters.title: Colonel Weiss
chapters.summary: Weiss's POV. The garrison commander, Colonel Weiss, inspects the archive and orders the most incriminating volumes crated first for the barges. A veteran who believes order requires forgetting, he senses someone in the town cares too much about paper. Emotional beat: cold conviction; the antagonist's logic made almost sympathetic.

chapters.title: Night Shift
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Tomas volunteers for night shifts alone with the presses, memorizing the guards' rotations and copying a key impression in wax. He is nearly caught by a drunk sergeant and covers by claiming he was fixing a jammed roller. Emotional beat: terror and exhilaration; a boy growing up fast.

chapters.title: The Name in the Margins
chapters.summary: Brandt's POV. Sorting crates, Brandt finds the report he falsified seven years ago — a massacre recorded as 'engagement losses.' He steals the page and confesses everything to Ines at the orchard house. Emotional beat: confession as release; shame beginning to turn toward atonement.

chapters.title: Betrayal in the Canteen
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. A garrison laundress who has seen Ines near the records room trades information to the military police for extra rations. Ines is questioned and released for lack of proof, but the workshop is placed under stricter guard and Weiss doubles the watch. Emotional beat: paranoia closing in; trust becomes a liability.

chapters.title: Marek's Hands
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Old Marek, broken by the requisition, tells Tomas the workshop's history — how it printed the town's first free newspaper — and gives him the original typeface molds hidden in the cellar. 'Paper burns,' he says, 'but letters remember.' Emotional beat: inheritance; grief giving way to legacy.

chapters.title: The Plan on Apple Paper
chapters.summary: All three conspirators' POVs interleaved. In the orchard house they finalize the plan: on the night before demolition, Tomas will open the press, Brandt will unlock the records room, and Ines will set the names in type — every one of them. Emotional beat: resolve crystallizing; hope that feels like recklessness.

chapters.title: Weiss Suspects
chapters.summary: Weiss's POV. Weiss reviews the laundress's claims and orders the barge moved up two days, ahead of the thaw. He interrogates Brandt casually over cards, probing for cracks. Brandt holds, barely. Emotional beat: the noose tightening; the reader learns the deadline just shortened.

chapters.title: The Thaw Begins
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Cracks spider across the river ice; the town hears it groan at night. Soldiers celebrate the coming spring while Ines counts hours. She visits the graves behind the hospital and reads the blank stones aloud, filling them with names from memory. Emotional beat: elegy and urgency braided together.

chapters.title: Locked Doors
chapters.summary: Brandt's POV. On the eve of demolition, Brandt discovers the records room lock has been changed. Panicked, he improvises: he will report a fire hazard and get the crates moved to the loading dock early — outside, unguarded for one hour. Emotional beat: desperation breeding audacity.

chapters.title: The Night of Names
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs, rapid cuts. The plan unfolds: Brandt's ruse works, Tomas fires the ancient press, and Ines sets type by lamplight — Voss, and hundreds more. Guards approach twice; twice the press falls silent. At dawn the pages run wet and warm. Emotional beat: breathless suspense breaking into fierce joy.

chapters.title: What the River Carried
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. As the ice breaks, the town wakes to find the true casualty list nailed to doors, tucked in market baskets, pressed into hymnals. The barges depart carrying only blank ledgers. Weiss rages but cannot arrest a whole town. Emotional beat: triumph shadowed by cost — the workshop is dynamited at noon.

chapters.title: Ash and Apples
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Standing in the workshop's ashes, Tomas buries the typeface molds in the orchard rather than surrender them. Marek weeps freely for the first time. The three conspirators say goodbye carefully, never naming what they did. Emotional beat: mourning and quiet pride; endings that are also seeds.

chapters.title: The Inquiry
chapters.summary: Brandt's POV. An army inquiry arrives; Brandt confesses to the falsified report of seven years ago, taking the weight onto himself so the others stay invisible. He is stripped of rank and imprisoned briefly, and walks out lighter than he went in. Emotional beat: sacrifice completed; guilt finally paid down.

chapters.title: Her Own Name
chapters.summary: Ines's POV, epilogue. One year later, in a rebuilt corner of the orchard house, Ines opens a new ledger and begins recording the town's restored honor roll — then, at the end, writes her own name for the first time. Tomas sets it in type. Emotional beat: peace earned; memory kept alive by chosen family.
